claims.text: Rapid high-energy Joule heating produces disordered HEA nanoparticles with non-equilibrated atomic distributions.
The proposed intervention is a roughly 10 °C/min ramp to about 300 °C, a 10-minute hold, and rapid quenching to room temperature.
An intermediate-temperature hold enhances local atomic mobility and short-range interdiffusion.
Enhanced interdiffusion during the hold stabilizes a single-phase HEA nanoparticle over phase-separation and segregation pathways.
The hold enables atoms to overcome kinetic barriers and mix uniformly.
Limiting atomic motion during the hold avoids phase separation while still permitting mixing.
The diffusion stage promotes entropy stabilization by balancing enthalpic interactions that would otherwise drive segregation.
The controlled thermal profile will yield a more homogeneous, single-phase structure, potentially FCC, than a rapid one-step profile.
The controlled thermal profile will reduce elemental segregation relative to the rapid-process baseline.
The controlled thermal profile will produce a narrower particle-size distribution than the rapid-process baseline.
A rapid one-step heating–cooling process typically produces elemental segregation, phase separation, and broad particle-size distributions.
The hypothesis applies to fixed-composition noble-metal HEA nanoparticles containing more than five elements, with Au, Ag, Pd, Pt, and Ru given as examples.
The hold temperature must remain below the decomposition or unwanted-transition threshold while being high enough to promote atomic mixing.
Temperature or hold-duration choices outside the applicable window may fail to improve phase homogeneity.
Rapid cooling can preserve the single-phase nanoparticle structure and small particle size.
Rapid cooling can hinder phase separation and favor a homogeneous elemental distribution.
The optimal hold temperature and duration may depend on composition and precursor chemistry.
The diffusion kinetics controlling mixing versus segregation have not been precisely quantified.

Failure of the held samples to show a statistically significant improvement in phase homogeneity and segregation relative to an identical-composition rapid-process control would falsify the hypothesis.
